Learning Objectives
Assess the indications for various surgical treatment options in patients with ankle arthritis.
Determine surgical techniques associated with each treatment option.
Outline common complications associated with the surgical management of ankle arthritis,
and review current treatment strategies.
Surgical Management
Anterior Decompression/Cheilectomy
Involves ankle debridement with anterior tibial/dorsal talar exostectomy (Figure 1)


Anterior Decompressions/Cheilectomy
Anterior decompression of the ankle is indicated in patients with anterior ankle joint line
pain and osteophytes observed on radiographs in whom degenerative changes do not
extend posteriorly into the ankle joint. Patients often have discomfort, particularly with
dorsiflexion maneuvers, such as squatting or ascending inclines. Surgical decompression
may relieve pain during these maneuvers by removing the bony impingement; however,
this procedure does not affect the natural history of disease progression, and patients
should be counseled that symptoms may worsen because of increased tibiotalar motion
and progressive arthritic wear deep in the ankle joint. In addition, anterior
decompression should not be performed in patients with anterior subluxation of the
talus because removal of the osteophytes may worsen this subluxation and symptoms. If
performed via an open approach, medial and/or lateral incisions may be required based
on the exact location of the osteophytes; however, consideration should be made (with
SEND FEEDBACK

respect to incision placement) for potential future procedures (ie, straight anterior
incision to facilitate later total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) or ankle arthrodesis).
Supramalleolar Osteotomy
Indicated in patients who have mild or moderate ankle arthritis with tibiotalar malalignment
and eccentric articular wear
Purpose is to offload arthritic areas and redistribute the joint load onto intact articular
cartilage.
Options include opening wedge, closing wedge, or dome osteotomies, with or without fibular
osteotomy.

Supramalleolar Osteotomy
Supramalleolar osteotomy should be considered in patients with ankle arthritis that is
mild or moderate (ie, not severe) if the surgeon believes that correction of a tibiotalar
joint deformity or distal tibia deformity may prolong the need for definitive ankle joint–
sacrificing procedures. Other indications include a deformity in the distal tibia that
requires correction before a definitive ankle arthritis procedure (eg, TAA).
Typically, varus deformity is corrected via a medial opening wedge tibial osteotomy (a
fibular osteotomy may be necessary for corrections >10°) (Figure 2). Typically, valgus
deformity is managed via a medial closing wedge osteotomy and may require an oblique
lengthening fibular osteotomy. Dome osteotomy of the distal tibia (with or without
fibular osteotomy) also is an option and results in less secondary translation than
opening or closing wedge osteotomies. These osteotomies typically require internal
fixation; however, gradual correction with the use of a thin-wire external fixator is an
option for larger or multiplanar deformities. Complications of supramalleolar osteotomy
include nonunion (particularly with opening wedge osteotomies), malunion, under
correction, overcorrection, and progression of arthritis. The position of the hindfoot and
forefoot should be carefully analyzed preoperatively because malalignment may be
present that will need to be managed via concomitant procedures to correct foot
deformity (Resource 1).

Distraction arthroplasty involves using a multiplanar external fixator to distract the ankle joint
and, theoretically, allow for biologic repair of subchondral bone; however, the exact
mechanism of action is unknown (Figure 3).

Indications are congruent ankle joint, no angular deformity, preserved motion, and no more
than moderate ankle arthritis (mild arthritis associated with better outcomes); however, the
efficacy of this technique remains controversial.

Distraction Arthroplasty
Distraction arthroplasty typically is considered in younger patients with ankle arthritis
who are not candidates for a joint-sacrificing procedure, such as TAA, and/or who have
reservations about undergoing ankle arthrodesis. A patient must have well-maintained
preoperative ankle motion for this technique to be considered. Static distraction and
hinged distraction, which allows for motion in the external fixator, have been described.2
Intermediate to long-term results are variable, with one study reporting 84% ankle joint
survival at median follow-up of 5 years and another study reporting only 55% of native
ankle joints present at mean follow-up of 8 years.3,4 Patients experiencing failure had
radiographs demonstrating progression of ankle arthritis. Therefore, patients should be
counseled regarding expectations, the long-term results of this procedure, and the
possible need for future surgery (Resource 2).
Ankle Arthrodesis
Indications
End-stage ankle arthritis (Resource 3)
Posttraumatic ankle arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
Tibiotalar deformity
Osteonecrosis

Ankle Arthrodesis
Arthrodesis is an effective treatment option for the management of end-stage
arthritis of the ankle and, historically, has been the preferred treatment option.
However, TAA has become increasingly prevalent as a viable treatment option.
Although both treatment options afford excellent pain relief, advantages and
SEND FEEDBACK

disadvantages are associated with each procedure. Ankle arthrodesis sacrifices
tibiotalar motion, resulting in pain relief and stability. Patients experience
considerable functional improvements compared with their preoperative status;
however, loss of motion may influence gait; walking speed; and accommodation of
uneven ground, such as inclines, declines, and stairs. The decision to perform ankle
arthrodesis (rather than TAA) must be individualized to each patient, and expectations
must be discussed in detail (Video 2)

Postoperative management
Patients typically are instructed to remain non–weight bearing for 6 to 8 weeks
postoperatively.
Immobilization is surgeon dependent but typically involves a splint and/or cast for 6 weeks
postoperatively, followed by transition to a walking boot until 10 to 12 weeks postoperatively.
Supportive shoes with rocker-bottom soles are used after the patient is transitioned out of
the boot.
Patients who undergo ankle arthrodesis typically do not require formal physical therapy.
Complications
Adjacent joint arthritis
Nonunion
Malunion
Infection

Ankle Arthrodesis
Ankle arthrodesis techniques (surgical approach and fixation methods) have evolved
over the past several decades. Regardless of the approach selected, achieving optimal
ankle positioning is critical. The recommended position of the ankle for arthrodesis is
neutral in the sagittal plane, no more than 5° of hindfoot valgus, and rotation equal to
the contralateral limb. Arthroscopic fusion or mini-arthrotomy techniques may be
considered in patients with minimal preexisting ankle deformity requiring correction.
Fixation via these techniques typically is achieved with the use of two or three large,
cannulated screws with variable configurations. Some studies have reported improved
outcomes with arthroscopic techniques compared with open techniques.5
Traditionally, the open technique involved the use of a lateral trans-fibular approach,
either sacrificing the fibula or using the fibula as a lateral strut graft. Currently, fibular
preservation is preferred to allow for potential conversion to TAA in the future (if
applicable). The anterior approach is now the approach preferred by many surgeons
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Ankle
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000004
13/33

because it allows for preservation of the fibula and anterior plating. In addition, it is the
most common approach used for future TAA. Posterior approaches also have been
described (typically via an Achilles-splitting approach) using posterior plate fixation.
Selecting an open approach often is secondary to the specific deformity, soft-tissue
considerations, or bone stock available for arthrodesis. For example, a lateral trans-
fibular approach may be helpful in the reduction of varus hindfoot deformity, whereas
an anterior approach with an anterior plate and a medial column trans-articular screw
may be helpful in the reduction of valgus hindfoot deformity. Thin-wire ring external
fixation can be used in patients undergoing complex ankle arthrodesis. Indications for
external fixation ankle arthrodesis include infected nonunion, soft-tissue envelope
compromise, the need for concomitant severe deformity correction, and bone transport
secondary to substantial bone loss.
Some patients may have concomitant subtalar joint arthritis as well as tibiotalar arthritis.
In these patients, the subtalar joint may be included in the arthrodesis construct,
creating a tibiotalocalcaneal arthrodesis. Plate fixation or retrograde intramedullary nail
fixation may be used for this surgical technique.
The most common long-term complication after ankle arthrodesis is adjacent joint
arthritis. The subtalar joint and talonavicular joint are most involved because of the
increased motion and stress these joints endure after successful ankle arthrodesis, even
if appropriate ankle alignment has been achieved. Although this adjacent arthritis is
observed radiographically, patients may or may not be symptomatic enough to require
additional surgical treatment.
The rate of nonunion after ankle arthrodesis is approximately 10%. Tobacco use
adversely affects healing time, with smokers having a 2.7 times greater risk of nonunion
and delayed healing versus nonsmokers. Most surgeons use some form of bone graft
(autograft, allograft, or biologic alternatives) to attempt to increase the rate of union.
Traditional management of ankle arthrodesis nonunion involves revision arthrodesis
with the use of bone graft; however, some surgeons have begun converting ankle
arthrodesis nonunions to TAA if no infection is present (Resource 4). Malunion is less
common than nonunion but may be similarly debilitating. The most problematic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000004
14/33

malpositioning of ankle arthrodesis is ankle plantar flexion. In this scenario, to place the
heel on the ground, the knee must be in recurvatum. This results in secondary knee
pathology because of the nonanatomic stress applied to the joint. Management may
require a closing wedge osteotomy through the ankle fusion site. Dorsiflexion malunion
may result in increased pressure on the heel pad and subsequent pain (Resource 5).
Varus malunion may result i painful lateral overload, particularly at the fifth metatarsal
base.
The rate of deep infection after ankle arthrodesis is relatively low; however, literature on
this topic is sparse. Deep infection often results in a nonunion that may necessitate
salvage via revision arthrodesis with the use of a thin-wire external fixation device.6
Total Ankle Arthroplasty
Indications
End-stage ankle arthritis
Posttraumatic ankle arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
Bilateral ankle degenerative joint disease (DJD)
Ankle DJD with concomitant hindfoot (subtalar, talonavicular) DJD or fusion
Contraindications
Absolute
Active infection or osteomyelitis
Extensive osteonecrosis of talus or tibia
Charcot neuroarthropathy
Inadequate bone stock that would not support the components of the prosthesis
Relative
Young age (<50 years; however, this is controversial)
Obesity
Considerable coronal plane deformity (also controversial and dependent on surgeon
experience)
Techniques
Approaches
Anterior approach (most implants)

Typically, a splint is applied initially; patients are transitioned to a cast or boot 2 to 3 weeks
postoperatively.
Compression wrapping with elevation decreases wound complications8 and may be
performed in combination with immediate physical therapy and range-of-motion exercises.
Length of non–weight bearing often depends on whether other foot procedures were
performed (may range from 2 to 6 weeks postoperatively).
Immobilization generally is continued until 10 to 12 weeks postoperatively.
Early range of motion and physical therapy may improve functional outcomes; however,
incisions must be well healed.
Complications
Aseptic loosening
Subsidence
Malalignment
Osteolysis
Infection
Gutter impingement
Arthrofibrosis

Total Ankle Arthroplasty
TAA has increased in popularity over the past few decades because of improvements in
implant design, instrumentation, and total ankle prosthesis longevity. Modern implants
are associated with greater than 90% short-term survivorship; however, survivorship
begins to decline at 8 to 14 years postoperatively (Figure 7). Multiple studies have
revealed substantial improvement in pain, functional activity, and patient-reported
outcomes compared with preoperative status. Compared with ankle arthrodesis, TAA
results in equivalent patient-reported outcomes and pain improvement and improved
functional activity, including measured range of motion (motion of adjacent joints rather
than ankle motion) and gait parameters (eg, measured range of motion, cadence, and
ability to manage inclines and declines) but a higher rate of revision surgery (Resource
6).

Indications for TAA are similar to those for ankle arthrodesis; however, more relative
indications and contraindications exist for TAA. In patients with bilateral ankle DJD,
concomitant hindfoot (subtalar and talonavicular joint) DJD, or prior hindfoot fusion, TAA
is preferred over ankle arthrodesis. Patient age must be carefully considered in selecting
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Ankle
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000004
19/33

TAA because of the expected longevity of the implant and the potential need for revision
surgery in the future. Historically, age younger than 50 years was a contraindication for
TAA; however, because TAA prostheses and instrumentation techniques have improved,
some surgeons are discussing this treatment option with patients younger than 50
years. A well-educated patient may elect to undergo TAA for the management of end-
stage ankle arthritis. Obesity has not been proven to be a contraindication to TAA;
however, additional large-scale and longer term studies are necessary. The ability to
correct coronal plane deformity via TAA also has evolved and is surgeon dependent. In
general, patients with varus deformities up to 20° to 30° may be considered for TAA,
whereas valgus deformities tend to be more difficult to correct (relative limit of 15°).
Again, surgeon experience is a key factor in considering these relative indications and
contraindications. The surgeon should have a thorough preoperative discussion with the
patient regarding risks and expectations (Resource 7).
The preferred approach for TAA is the anterior approach. The superficial peroneal nerve
is almost always present at the distal aspect of the incision and must be identified and
protected. Dissection is carried deep to the extensor retinaculum, most commonly
between the tibialis anterior tendon and the extensor hallucis longus tendon, avoiding
the deep neurovascular bundle. Currently, only one system is available that involves a
lateral approach via a fibular osteotomy.
Each TAA system has specific instruments and steps that must be followed to ensure
correct placement. Regardless of specific instrumentation, good alignment in the
coronal, sagittal, and axial planes with regard to the mechanical axis of the leg is critical.
Other concepts that must be understood and addressed include achieving good anterior
coverage of the cut tibial surface, avoiding too wide of a talar implant that may result in
medial and lateral gutter impingement, and performing adequate medial and lateral
gutter débridement. After the implant is placed, good sagittal range of motion should be
confirmed, and coronal plane stability must be assessed (and addressed if unstable).
Fixed-bearing and mobile-bearing devices are available. The terms refer to whether the
polyethylene component is fixed to the tibial component or can move independent of it.
Currently, some literature suggests an advantage to fixed-bearing devices; however,
additional studies are necessary.7 Some surgeons advocate against mobile-bearing

9/3/26, 7:22 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000004
20/33

designs in patients with considerable coronal plane deformity or anterior talar
translation (Video 4).
Video 4 Clanton TO: Mobile bearing vs fixed bearing implants: Differences and
similarities, from Haddad SL, mod: Total ankle arthroplasty: Understanding the
technological revolution in managing end stage ankle arthritis. Presented at the Annual
Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 13-
15, 2019.
Concomitant procedures often are necessary during TAA (Video 5). If equinus
contracture is present, then gastrocnemius recession or Achilles tendon lengthening
may be required. Lateral ankle ligament reconstruction is necessary in patients with
varus instability that is not corrected by increasing polyethylene thickness. Calcaneal
osteotomies, midfoot osteotomies, and hindfoot or midfoot fusion may be required to
manage cavovarus foot deformity or flatfoot deformities in patients with ankle arthritis.
Surgeons also must anticipate deformities that may require correction after coronal
plane deformity of the ankle is corrected. In patients with a larger deformity, the surgeon
must decide if these additional procedures should be performed concomitantly or in a
staged fashion (Resource 8). Prophylactic fixation of the medial malleolus should be
considered to prevent acute intraoperative and postoperative stress fractures of the
medial malleolus based on the width of the medial malleolus after implantation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:22 AM
AAOS | Arthritides of the Ankle
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000004
21/33

Video 5 Haddad SL: Deformity correction in total ankle arthroplasty in 2019, from
Haddad SL, mod: Total ankle arthroplasty: Understanding the technological revolution in
managing end stage ankle arthritis. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 13-15, 2019.
The revision rate after TAA is higher than after ankle arthrodesis, with failure rates of
10% to 20% being reported within 10 years after TAA.9 The most common reasons for
revision of TAA components are aseptic loosening (loosening of the components without
evidence for deep infection) and subsidence. Subsidence is observed as settling of the
tibial or talar components on serial radiographs. Malalignment of the implants or failure
to correct coronal plane deformity may lead to edge loading on the polyethylene
component, increased wear, and ultimate failure because of component loosening.
Osteolysis and peri-implant cyst formation are early and late complications of TAA. The
cause of osteolysis has yet to be fully defined; however, it is likely a combination of stress
shielding and bone remodeling after insertion and a macrophage-led immune response
to wear particles (Figures 10, 11, and 12). Symptomatic cysts that are becoming
progressively larger (or are located in a potentially catastrophic location) should be
managed surgically via bone grafting or revision of the implants, whereas asymptomatic
cysts can be monitored via serial radiographs and CT scans (Resource 9).

Deep infection rates after TAA are relatively low (<3%) but may be difficult for the patient
and may result in amputation. Early infection can be managed via aggressive
débridement and polyethylene exchange. Chronic or late infection should be managed
via débridement and removal of the implants, with staged conversion to arthrodesis or
revision if infection can be cleared. Gutter impingement and arthrofibrosis are relatively
common complications, especially early postoperatively; however, they typically result in
less morbidity. In symptomatic patients, gutter débridement, arthrolysis, and possible
Achilles tendon lengthening or gastrocnemius recession may be effective surgical
treatment options.
TAA failure is a difficult problem to manage. If adequate bone stock remains, then
revision TAA is the preferred treatment option. In patients with poor bone stock and
patients who have undergone multiple attempts at revision, conversion to arthrodesis is
